trans-unit.source: The input data that defines the strength of the biome to add. These values should be in the range of 0 to 1.
A planet modifier that lets you add biomes to the planet. Connect this modifier's data output to the biome input of a Biomes modifier to define a biome.
A planet modifier that adds a color value to the planet vertex data.
A planet modifier that adds a height (elevation) value to the planet vertex data.
The height, in meters, to add to the planet or biome.
A planet modifier that defines sub-biomes for a biome based on the altitude of the terrain.

The height (in meters) the current height can vary by when determining which sub-biome it belongs to. This doesn't change the actual height, just adds variation to the sub-biomes' height ranges. The strength of this variation is set by the height variance data input value, which multiplies this value.

The min and max heights, in meters, defining the range over which height variance reaches full strength. At or below the min, no variance applies. Above the max, variance applies 100%. Between min and max, the variance strength (set by the data input value) scales linearly from 0% to 100%.
If height variance is used, this input data defines the strength of the height variance (typically a value between 0 and 1).
If running in a biome specific pass, this determines whether the input data value comes from the common pass or from this biome specific pass.
The list of sub-biomes and their associated data defined for this biome.
The altitude range (in meters) for this sub-biome, defined by min and max heights. The min/max values should overlap neighboring sub-biomes for a smooth transition between them.
A planet modifier that applies data from a biome to the planet vertex data.
A planet modifier used to perform basic math operations on one or two data input values.

The range of input values reassigned to this biome. Biome ranges are ordered and evaluated by their min values. One range's max value should overlap the next range's min value so biomes transition smoothly. Input values outside all ranges are still reassigned: low values to the first biome range, high values to the last.
The maximum value to which the output value will be clamped.
The minimum value to which the output value will be clamped.
The data input value to be clamped.
The clamped output value, which should be between the specified minimum and maximum value.
A planet modifier that clamps a data value to a specified range.

Defines detached cloud layers that are rendered on dedicated transparent spheres around the planet in scaled space. Each layer reads its density from a data slot produced by the planet generation modifiers, and has its own height, tint and rotation speed. Order the layers by altitude (Low has the smallest height, High the largest) so higher layers correctly shadow the ones below them. The fourth layer is a non-rotating mask that multiplies the opacity of the other layers.
How finely the close-up detail noise tiles on this layer in the ground-level cloud view (higher is finer). Has no effect on the view from space.
Multiplies this layer's rotation speed to set how fast its close-up detail drifts and rotates in the ground-level cloud view. Has no effect on the view from space.
How strongly the close-up detail noise erodes this layer's edges in the ground-level cloud view (0 to ~0.6). Has no effect on the view from space.
The height of the cloud layer above sea level, in meters.
The data slot (produced by the planet generation modifiers) that this layer reads its density from. Set to -1 to disable the layer.
The data slot for a non-rotating mask that multiplies the opacity of the cloud layers, so clouds can be confined to certain regions. Set to -1 to disable.
How strongly the mask layer affects this layer's opacity (0 = ignore the mask, 1 = fully masked). Use low values for high clouds and high values for fog.
The rotation speed of the layer in radians per second, applied in addition to the planet's own rotation.

Reduces the cloud mask based on the planet's position in its orbit for a seasonal effect (0 disables it). Negative values thin the clouds most at the closest point to the parent (periapsis) and least at the farthest (apoapsis); positive values do the reverse. Only affects planets that use a cloud mask.
How strongly this layer follows the terrain height, lifting it over high ground so low clouds do not clip into elevated terrain (0 = flat shell, 1 = fully follows the terrain).
The thickness of the cloud layer in meters, giving it a visible vertical extent when flying through it in the ground-level cloud view. Has no effect on the view from space.
The color of the clouds. The alpha channel acts as an overall opacity multiplier.
The input data value which identifies which color band(s) will be used. For gas giants, this is typically the y-coordinate on a Unit sphere.
A planet modifier that produces color bands based on a data value.
The maximum expected input value. With the minimum, this sets the expected range of the input data value to remap it into the zero-to-one range.
The minimum expected input value. Used with the maximum to determine the input data's expected range and remap it into the zero-to-one range.
The color value to be blended in to the existing color.
An optional input specifying a data value to use as the source alpha channel, instead of the alpha defined in the source color.
A planet modifier that blends two colors together based on a data value.
The blend type used for the destination color (the existing color before this modifier is applied). This essentially selects the value by which the destination color will be multiplied.
The blend type used for the source color (specified in this modifier). This is essentially selecting the value by which the source color will be multiplied.
The inner angle (in degrees) based on a vector through the center of the pole.
The output value (before noise and remapping) that is used leading up to and including the inner angle.
The outer angle (in degrees) based on a vector through the center of the pole.
The output value (before noise and remapping) that is used at the outer angle and beyond.
The input data value that provides noise to the polar cap mask.
If enabled, the linear remapping will be clamped in the range of zero to one. If disabled, output values could exceed the zero to one range.
The maximum value used to remap the output value in the range of zero to one.
The minimum value used to remap the output value in the range of zero to one.
The noise strength that is used leading up to and including the inner angle.
The noise strength that is used at the outer angle and beyond.
This provides an easy way to quickly disable a crater pass, which can be useful in development and testing.
The frequency of the noise that generates the craters. The higher the frequency the smaller and more numerous the craters become.
The maximum depth of the crater in meters. This occurs when the crater shape curve evaluates to -1 on the y-axis.

The value used to linearly interpolate the crater shape noise between data inputs 'A' and 'B'. At 0, only input 'A' provides noise to the crater shapes. At 1, only input 'B' is used. Any value between 0 and 1 interpolates between the two.
The scalar value used to adjust the strength of the crater shape noise before it is applied.
The randomness in the crater position noise. Less randomness means more consistent (and larger) craters but they will be more grid like in alignment.
The rotation angle applied to the input position used to sample crater positions and sizes. Sometimes adjusting it slightly helps when multiple passes all want to pile craters on top of each other.

The axis of the rotation angle applied to the input position used to sample crater positions and sizes. Sometimes adjusting the rotation slightly helps when multiple passes all want to pile craters on top of each other.
The seed value used for the cellular noise that generates the crater positions and sizes.

The curve that craters resemble. Typically mapped between (0,-1) and (1,0). The x-axis is distance from the crater center, the y-axis is crater depth. The left side, starting at 0, is the crater center; the right side, typically ending at 1, is the end of the crater rims. The bottom, starting at -1, is the deepest part; the top, ending at 0, is the planet's regular surface.
The frequency of the noise that generates the crater positions and sizes. The higher the frequency, the smaller and more numerous the craters become.

The data input that, if used, can mask out the craters this modifier generates. Typically a value between zero and one, where one means full-strength unmasked craters and zero means this modifier changes nothing.
The exponent applied to the crater positional noise. This is used to help prevent seams between craters.

The strength of the crater shape noise. This noise adds variation to crater shapes so they aren't perfectly circular. The crater shape noise is highly configurable, and this value provides an easy way to adjust its final strength.

The number of crater passes to perform. Crater passes are expensive, so use them sparingly; however, multiple crater passes are cheaper than the same number of single-pass crater modifiers for a similar effect. Craters within a pass can't overlap, but craters in different passes can.
A planet modifier that generates terrain crater features.

The data output that, if used, holds the summed crater height noise from all passes. Multiplied by the crater max depth and the final crater strength, it gives the final height adjustment this modifier applies. Not always useful, but it can be. For example, with a single-pass crater, this value can pinpoint where craters are, so you can feed it into a biome modifier to generate biomes inside and outside craters.
The red, green, and blue color values (0 to 1) to add to the terrain color as the crater extends above the planet's surface. Useful for adding a bit of color variation to the crater rims.
The red, green, and blue color values (0 to 1) to subtract from the terrain color as it reaches the craters' minimum height. Useful for adding a bit of color variation to the deep centers of craters.

The first crater shape noise input data. Each crater pass can choose a value by which this noise input and the other are linearly interpolated to generate that pass's crater shape noise value. This adds variation so craters don't all appear as perfect circles. Lower frequency noise (relative to the crater size) can create some very interesting non-crater-like terrain.

The second crater shape noise input. Each crater pass picks a value used to linearly interpolate this noise input and the other to generate that pass's crater shape noise. This noise adds variation so craters don't all look like perfect circles. Lower frequency noise (relative to crater size) can create some very interesting non-crater-like terrain.

The default curve that craters resemble. Individual passes can override this; passes without a custom curve fall back to it. Typically mapped between (0,-1) and (1,0). The x-axis is distance from the crater center, the y-axis is crater depth. The left side, starting at 0, is the crater center; the right side, typically ending at 1, is the end of the crater rims. The bottom, starting at -1, is the deepest part; the top, ending at 0, is the planet's regular surface.
A fast planet modifier that generates terrain crater features.
An optional data output that stores the minimum noise output used for the height of the craters.
Prevents the seed from being randomized when the randomize button is clicked.
The red, green, and blue color values (typically 0 to 1) to add to the terrain color as the crater rises above the planet's surface. Useful for adding a bit of color variation to crater rims.

The red, green, and blue color values (typically 0 to 1) to subtract from the terrain color as it reaches the craters' minimum height. Useful for adding a bit of color variation to the deep centers of craters.
Allows multiple, unlocked Noise elements to obtain the same seed when the randomize button is clicked.

A planet modifier that reads data from a cubemap texture for the celestial body and stores an output value based on that data. The cubemap texture should be in horizontal format (X+, X-, Y+, Y-, Z+, Z-).

The interpolation method used when sampling the texture data. Bilinear should be much faster. Bicubic should be smoother, but won't always look better than bilinear, since the look depends heavily on the texture content and resolution. Stick with bilinear for performance unless bicubic offers a far better visual result.
The color gradient used in planet studio when using a brush on this cubemap.
The cubemap display name associated with this modifier (if any). This is required for using the brush flyout with this cubemap modifier.

The output value is linearly interpolated between the min and max values based on the texture data's pixel value. This also sets the maximum value of the source data when generating a default cubemap.

The output value is linearly interpolated between the min and max value based on the texture data's pixel value. This also defines the minimum value of the source data when generating a default cubemap.

The bits per pixel used at runtime to represent the texture data. A value of 32 can be slightly more efficient on the CPU but uses far more memory at runtime, especially for large textures. It's recommended to leave this at 8 bits per pixel.
The texture channel from which values should be used for this texture.
The debug color used to identify the X-negative face of the cubemap.
The debug color used to identify the X-positive face of the cubemap.
The debug color used to identify the Y-negative face of the cubemap.
The debug color used to identify the Y-positive face of the cubemap.
The debug color used to identify the Z-negative face of the cubemap.
The debug color used to identify the Z-positive face of the cubemap.
A debug planet modifier that visualizes the cubemap faces of the planet.
The input data to visualize. This value will be linearly interpolated between the min and max values specified by this modifier, then color will be applied based on the specified gradient.
A debug planet modifier that visualizes a data value on the planet surface.
A debug planet modifier that visualizes the biome data on the planet surface.
The amplitude of the domain warping noise.
The domain warping type. Domain warping adjusts the input position before generating the actual noise, thus 'warping' it. Some types use additional noise to perform the warping.
The frequency of the domain warping noise.
The gain of the domain warping noise.
The interpolation method of the domain warping noise. Linear is the fastest and lowest quality. Quintic is the slowest and best quality.
The lacunarity of the domain warping noise.
The number of octaves for the domain warping noise.

trans-unit.source: The X,Y,Z offset to apply to the input position before generating the noise value for that position.
The euler angles, in degrees, to rotate the input position before generating the noise value for that position.
The noise seed value used for the domain warping noise.
The amount of twist (in degrees) to apply to the lines in a single hemisphere.
The axis around which to apply the twisting.
The exponent to apply to the twist amount. Increasing this can reduce the twisting near the equator and increase the twisting near the poles.

How the twist strength at a given position is determined. Distance On Axis - twisting increases as distance along the axis increases. Distance On Axis Inverse - twisting decreases as distance along the axis increases. Distance From Axis - twisting increases as distance from the axis increases. Distance From Axis Inverse - twisting decreases as distance from the axis increases.
The X,Y,Z scale to apply to the input position before generating the noise value for that position.
The data output of the expression.
A planet modifier that evaluates a mathematical expression using data values as inputs.
The data input values to act as a mask. At 1.0, the terrain is completely flattened, fading out to the original height at 0.0.
A planet modifier that flattens the terrain in an area.
The height, in meters, to which the terrain should be flattened.
If enabled, the input value will have a smoothstep function applied to it before use as a flatten mask.
The input data value that is used to generate the heights.
The data output that stores the generated height data.
A planet modifier that generates height data for the planet terrain.

How the data input is interpreted to generate a height output. Lerp Min To Max: height is linearly interpolated from minimum to maximum based on the input value and its specified range. Lerp To/From Zero: height is linearly interpolated from minimum to zero if the input is negative, or from zero to maximum if positive. Don't use this if the minimum and maximum heights don't span across zero.
The maximum input value used to create the range by which the input value will be linearly interpolated.
The minimum input value used to create the range by which the input value will be linearly interpolated.
The maximum height (in meters) generated by this modifier.
The minimum height (in meters) generated by this modifier.
The output in which to store the biome strength (a value between 0 and 1).
A planet modifier that reads the strength of a specific biome into a data value.
The output in which to store the combined biome strength (typically a value between 0 and 1).
A planet modifier that reads the combined strength of all biomes into a data value.
The data from the common pass that is to be stored in the biome specific pass data channel.
The biome specific pass data output.
A planet modifier that reads data from the common pass into the current pass data.
The data output to store the constant value.
A planet modifier that writes a constant value into a data slot.
The constant value to store in the data output.
The output data to contain the strength of the current biome (typically a value between 0 and 1).
A planet modifier that reads the strength of the current biome into a data value.
The data output used to store the requested height value (in meters).
A planet modifier that reads the current terrain height into a data slot.

The type of height value to retrieve. Default: the common height in a non-biome pass, the biome height in a biome pass. Common Height: the common height, regardless of pass. Biome Height: the biome height in a biome pass; retrieves the common height if run in a non-biome pass. Combined Height: biome height plus common height in a biome pass; retrieves the common height if run in a non-biome pass.
If enabled, the radius of the celestial body will be added to the output of the modifier. This is typically not enabled.
The data output used to store the X-position value.
The data output used to store the Y-position value.
The data output used to store the Z-position value.
A planet modifier that reads the current vertex position into data slots.
The rotation in degrees about the X, Y, and Z axis to be applied to the planet before returning the requested positions.
A planet modifier that swaps biomes between hemispheres.
The 'A' input to be interpolated. The result will be interpolated from input 'A' to input 'B'.
The 'B' input to be interpolated. The result will be interpolated from input 'A' to input 'B'.

The value used to interpolate between the two inputs. Below the min input value, the output is input 'A'. Above the max input value, the output is input 'B'. In between, the output is interpolated based on where this value falls in the specified min/max range.
A planet modifier that interpolates between two values based on a factor.
The maximum input value used to create the range for the interpolation value input.
The minimum input value used to create the range for the interpolation value input.

The exponent to which the interpolation value is raised after remapping it into the 0 to 1 range based on the min/max input values. A value of 1 gives linear interpolation. A value above or below one makes interpolation occur over a curve.
A planet modifier that defines biomes arranged in horizontal layers.

Determines how the input is converted to biomes. Single Biome - The input value is the primary biome's strength, from 0% at 0 to 100% at 1. Dual Biome Negative And Positive - The input value represents two biomes. The primary biome's strength runs from 0 (0%) to 1 (100%); the other biome's from 0 (0%) to -1 (100%). Dual Biome Positive And Remainder - The input value represents two biomes. The primary biome's strength runs from 0 (0%) to 1 (100%); the other biome's strength is 100% minus the primary's.

trans-unit.source: The 'A' input to be interpolated. The result will be interpolated from input 'A' to input 'B'.
The 'B' input to be interpolated. The result will be interpolated from input 'A' to input 'B'.

The value used to interpolate between the two inputs. If this value is below the min input value, the output will be input 'A'. If this value is above the max input value, the output will be input 'B'. If this value is in between those two values, the output will be linearly interpolated based on where this value falls between zero and one.
A planet modifier that linearly interpolates a value from range A to range B, mapping it to the 0-1 range.

The optional noise input applied to the lines. The input value is used as longitude variation in degrees, so a value of 1 shifts a line's output position by one degree. Typically this input comes from a noise modifier with a strength value of 'x' degrees.
The output data representing the lines calculated by this modifier. This should be in the range of zero (no lines) to 1 (center of line).
A planet modifier that generates longitude lines on the planet surface.
The number of lines to be generated by this modifier.
The width of the lines, in degrees, generated by this modifier.
The rotation in degrees about the X, Y, and Z axis to be applied to the input position.
The amplitude of the domain warping noise applied to the input.
The frequency of the domain warping noise applied to the input.
The gain applied to the amplitude at each octave of the domain warping noise applied to the input.
The lacunarity applied to the frequency at each octave of the domain warping noise applied to the input.
The number of octaves used in the domain warping noise applied to the input.
The output data value representing the polar caps. The north pole mask runs from zero to 1, the south pole mask from 0 to -1.
A planet modifier that generates a mask for the polar cap regions of the planet.
A planet modifier that flattens terrain radially around a point.
The falloff power used when interpolating between the target elevation and original elevation.

The inner radius, in meters, of the terrain to flatten. All terrain within this radius is set to the specified elevation. The elevation is interpolated back to non-flattened terrain from the inner radius to the outer radius.
The latitude and longitude of the center point of the radial flatten.

The outer radius, in meters, of the terrain to flatten. All terrain beyond it is unaffected by this modifier. Elevation is interpolated from flattened to non-flattened terrain between the inner and outer radius.
Use the Smooth Step function instead of a falloff power curve. If selected, then Falloff Power will be ignored.
The data input values to be remapped.
The output results of the modifier.
A planet modifier that remaps a data value using an animation curve.
The curve used to remap the input values. The X-axis represents the input values and the Y-axis defines the values they will be remapped to.
A planet modifier that linearly remaps a data value from one range to another.

The maximum value of the range from which values are remapped. Input values at or beyond this are remapped to 'To Max Value'. Input values between 'From Min Value' and this are linearly interpolated between 'To Min Value' and 'To Max Value'.

The minimum value of the range that values are remapped from. Input values at or below this remap to 'To Min Value'. Input values between this and 'From Max Value' are linearly interpolated between 'To Min Value' and 'To Max Value'.

The maximum value of the range to which values are remapped. Input values at or beyond 'From Max Value' remap to this. Input values between 'From Min Value' and 'From Max Value' are linearly interpolated between 'To Min Value' and this.

The minimum value of the range that values are remapped to. Input values at or below 'From Min Value' remap to this. Input values between 'From Min Value' and 'From Max Value' are linearly interpolated between this and 'To Max Value'.
A planet modifier that linearly remaps a data value using a mirrored dual range.

The maximum value of the range from which values are remapped. Input values at or beyond this are remapped to 'To Max Value'. Input values between 'From Min Value' and this are linearly interpolated between 'To Min Value' and 'To Max Value'. These results are mirrored about zero when the input is below zero.

The minimum value of the range being remapped from. Input values at or below this are remapped to 'To Min Value'. Inputs between this and 'From Max Value' are linearly interpolated between 'To Min Value' and 'To Max Value'. Results are mirrored about zero when the input is below zero.

The maximum value of the range that values are remapped to. Input values at or beyond 'From Max Value' remap to this. Input values between 'From Min Value' and 'From Max Value' are linearly interpolated between 'To Min Value' and this. These results are mirrored about zero when the input is below zero.

The minimum value of the range that values are remapped to. Input values at or below 'From Min Value' remap to this. Input values between 'From Min Value' and 'From Max Value' are linearly interpolated between this and 'To Max Value'. Results are mirrored about zero when the input is below zero.

Marks which data slot holds the ISRU resource patchiness field (0..1). Author the value upstream with the normal noise/remap/combine modifiers; each sub-biome's Noise Strength slider then chooses how much of it to apply.
The data slot whose value (clamped to 0..1) is used as the ISRU resource patchiness field. Author it upstream with the noise/remap/combine modifiers. Leave unset (-1) for uniform resource coverage.

A planet modifier that defines a single sub-biome for a biome.

If enabled, input values beyond the final terrace section's 'Start Value' are clamped to that 'Start Value'. If disabled, input values exceeding the final 'Start Value' pass through untouched to the output.
If enabled, input values below the first terrace section's 'Start Value' are clamped to that 'Start Value'. If disabled, input values below the first 'Start Value' pass untouched to the output.
The data input value to convert to a terraced output value. This value can be in any range, as long as the corresponding start values for each section use the same range.

The percentage of this terrace section that will be completely flat. The section extends from its start value to the next section's start value. This defines the percentage of that range where output is always set to this section's start value. The rest is the slope to the next terrace section.

The exponent defining how this terrace section's slope is interpolated from its start value to the next section's start value. A value of 1 results in linear interpolation of the slope from this section to the next.
The data input value at which this terrace section starts.
A planet modifier used to read data from a specific face of a cubemap texture and project it onto the planet surface.
A planet modifier used to read data from a texture and project it onto the planet surface using latitude/longitude coordinates.
The cube face of the texture's center position.

The interpolation method used when sampling the texture data. Bilinear should be much faster. Bicubic should be smoother, but won't always look better than bilinear, since the look depends heavily on the texture content and resolution as well as the texture's size on the celestial body. Stick with bilinear for performance unless bicubic offers a far better visual result.

The maximum value this texture generates, added to the modifier output for a max-value pixel. For example, if this is 100 and pixels range from 0 to 255, then a pixel of 0 generates 0, a pixel of 102 generates 40, and a pixel of 255 generates 100.
The position of the center of the texture on the cube face. Coordinates are unit cube space, from -0.5 to 0.5.
The rotation of the texture in degrees. NOTE: Only increments of 90 degrees will work.
The size of the texture relative to the cube face. Coordinates are unit cube space with a size value of 1 filling the entire cubemap face.

The interpolation method used when sampling the texture data. Bilinear should be much faster. Bicubic should be smoother, but won't always look better than bilinear, since the look depends heavily on the texture content and resolution as well as the projected texture size. Stick with bilinear for performance unless bicubic offers a far better visual result.

The longitude at which this texture data should be centered and projected onto the celestial body.
The texture data to be projected onto the celestial body.

The value range for this sub-biome, defined as min and max values from the input data that defines it. The min/max values should overlap neighboring sub-biomes for a smooth transition between them.
The method used to calculate distance when using cellular noise.
When using cellular noise, this determines what kind of values will be stored as the output of this modifier.
The output of this noise modifier. Many noise methods are capped between -1 and 1, but that is not always the case.
A highly configurable planet modifier that can be used to generate all sorts of noise.

Typically each octave scales the previous octave's amplitude by the 'Gain' value. If set to manual, the amplitude at each octave can be set to a specific value. This is an advanced technique, generally not recommended, but it can be very useful in some scenarios.

Typically each octave of noise scales the previous octave's frequency by the 'Lacunarity' value. If set to manual, the frequency at each octave can be set to a specific value. This is an advanced technique, generally not recommended, but it can be very useful in some scenarios.

For fractal-based noise, this sets the fractal type. They each behave in different, interesting ways. It's best to just experiment with each to get a feel for what they do and how the various settings affect them. Good luck!

If using fractal-with-derivative-based noise, this sets the type used. These all behave in different and interesting ways. It's best to experiment with each to get a feel for what they do and how the various settings affect them. Good luck!
The number of cycles per unit length.
A multiplier that determines how the strength changes with each successive octave.
The interpolation method used by the noise. Linear is the fastest and lowest quality. Quintic is the slowest and best quality.
A multiplier that determines how quickly the frequency increases for each successive octave.

The ID of the optional map for this modifier. If left blank, this brush flyout can't use this modifier to create custom painted maps. This should be a unique name within the celestial body being created.
If enabled and a cubemap is used, the regular noise will be combined with the cubemap noise. If false, only the cubemap noise value is returned.

If a custom cubemap is used, this sets the sampling mode for applying the map data to the planet. Bicubic generally looks better (not always), but it's much more expensive than Bilinear.
The optional data input used as a mask for this modifier. These values are typically 0 to 1 and scale the strength of the noise result.
The number of times to run the noise, each time modifying its frequency by lacunarity and its strength by gain. More octaves can improve visuals but reduce runtime performance.
The power exponent used in some noise types.
The seed value for the noise. Each unique seed should produce completely unique noise for a given set of configuration values.
The strength of the 'slope erosion' used by some noise types.

Adjusts how aggressive auto-pilot reacts to errors for the given axis. This may need to be lowered for highly maneuverable aircraft, or oscillations will occur.
Adjust these settings to fine-tune how the auto-pilot controls the craft.

Auto-pilot uses a "PID" controller with 3 components: Proportional, Integral, and Derivative. Adjust them in-flight to find optimal values (View Panel->Auto-Pilot), then set them here to save with the craft. The hard part of PID tuning is controlling oscillation when the craft is nearly on-target. Values should be large enough to produce the desired response rate without introducing oscillation, across a range of airspeeds. Any value, if too high, can cause oscillation.
To start tuning in flight: set integral and derivative to zero. Raise proportional until you reach the desired response rate with minimal oscillation (you may not eliminate it). Raise derivative until overshoot/oscillation is minimized. Add integral to fix any persistent error while keeping oscillation low. Tip: Display input sliders to monitor oscillation in inputs.
Used to reduce overshooting/oscillations, although excessive amounts will introduce oscillation. Highly maneuverable crafts will not tolerate much if any derivative without introducing oscillation.
Attempts to compensate for cases where the proportional is not sufficient to maintain the target. Not typically recommended for roll.

The primary value dictating how strongly the auto-pilot reacts to errors. Craft with large control lag need proportional reduced considerably below the craft's maximum rate to bring oscillation to an acceptable level.

trans-unit.source: The input axis driving this input controller.

A set of one, two, or three comma-separated numbers defining the input axis value range and how it remaps into the -1 to 1 range.
{max} - Input axis values <= 0 are remapped to zero. Values >= {max} are remapped to 1. Values between 0 and {max} are lerped between 0 and 1.
{min},{max} - Input axis values <= {min} are remapped to -1. Values >= {max} are remapped to 1. Values between {min} and {max} are lerped between -1 and 1.
{min},{zero},{max} - Input axis values <= {min} are remapped to -1. Values >= {max} are remapped to 1. Values between {min} and {zero} are lerped between -1 and 0. Values between {zero} and {max} are lerped between 0 and 1. If {min} and {zero} are equal, inputs <= {min} are remapped to 0. If {zero} and {max} are equal, inputs >= {max} are remapped to 0.

The Biomes flyout panel customizes the look of specific regions of your planet. Each biome is split into one or more sub-biomes, which define the visual style for different altitudes within the same biome.
For example, imagine a grassland biome split into three sub-biomes that define how it changes visually as altitude increases. The first could start at -500 meters, well below sea level, and extend to 10 meters above it, with a sandy color and texture to represent beaches near sea level. The next could extend to 500 meters with a grassy color and texture. The last could run from 500 to 10,000 meters with a gray color and rocky texture to represent mountains.

Looking closely at the diagram above, you'll notice each sub-biome overlaps by some amount. This overlap lets sub-biomes blend smoothly as they transition from one to another; the larger the overlap, the more gradual the transition.
Each sub-biome can also define a different visual style based on slope. This is useful for something like a mountain where steep faces are gray but flat spots are white. View each sub-biome's settings via the Flat Style and Slope Style buttons. The Flat End Angle and Slope Start Angle define the range over which those styles blend together.

Some planets define their sub-biomes by a value instead of a height, which requires the Sub-Biomes (Value Based) planet modifier for each biome. This can be more flexible and makes it easier to scale your planet's terrain features without changing sub-biome ranges, but it's harder to set up and less intuitive to work with.

The Celestial Body Designer is where you build custom celestial bodies (aka planets). Several flyout panels let you customize different parts of your planet.
The Properties flyout holds general info such as radius, gravity, atmosphere settings, and more. Settings are extensively tool-tipped, so read those for details on a particular setting.
Some settings apply immediately, but others require "rebuilding the planet," done via the Rebuild button in the Celestial Body inspector panel at the top right of the screen. When a rebuild is needed, the button turns blue, as shown below.

A planet modifier can pass data to another by writing it to a data slot. There are only 10 slots, and writing to one overwrites whatever was there.
In Advanced View, toggle the Data Flow panel to see how data flows between modifiers. In the example below, the Noise modifier writes to slot 3; the next modifier, BasicArithmetic, reads from slot 3 and writes its output to slot 4. Slot 3's data persists since BasicArithmetic didn't overwrite it. Blue blocks are outputs; U-shaped blocks are inputs.

Change which data slot a modifier uses for inputs and outputs by clicking and dragging its icons in the Data Flow panel. You can also change a modifier's inputs and outputs by selecting it and using the Data Slots section at the bottom of the inspector window.

There are two types of data slots: common and biome. During common passes, all planet modifiers write to and read from common data slots. In a biome pass, data is written to and read from a temporary set of slots that reset after each biome pass. A biome pass cannot write to common data slots, but it can read them with a GetCommonData modifier, which reads from a common data slot and outputs into a biome data slot.

A few planet modifiers help troubleshoot terrain generation. The Debug Visualization (Biomes) modifier overrides terrain color to show a distinct color per biome. Just place it at the end of the Final Pass and rebuild the planet.
The Debug Visualize (Data) modifier outputs color based on its input, using that input to look up a value in the customizable color gradient in its inspector panel. The input can come from any modifier, but often displays a Noise modifier's output. To use it, place it directly after a Noise modifier and set its input data slot to match the Noise modifier's output data slot. Here's an example showing output from a Noise modifier with a Perlin Fractal noise type.

It's also wise to watch your planet's performance via the Performance section of the Celestial Body inspector panel, noting the Quad Build Times, especially the average. Faster average build times improve the experience for players who download your planet. Load up the stock planets and note their average quad build times on your device, then compare. If your planet is considerably slower, it may be worth cutting back on the complexity of your planet modifiers. You can also tweak Properties -> Terrain Quality Modes to reduce the subdivisions and Terrain Vertices per quad.

Welcome to Planet Studio! Here you can build custom planets and planetary systems, then upload and share them with the community.
Planet Studio has two parts: the Celestial Body Designer and the Planetary System Designer. The Celestial Body Designer is where you build any celestial body — planets, suns, moons, dwarf planets, etc. Enter it via the Create Planet or Load Planet buttons in the menu.
The Planetary System Designer is where you build a solar system from celestial bodies saved on your device. Define their orbits and parent/child relationships. Once complete, upload your system to the website and share it with the community. Enter it via the Load System button in the menu.
Both Designers have configurable inputs for camera movement and more, which you can view and configure under Settings -> Control Settings -> Planet Studio.
Note: We often say planet instead of the more correct "celestial body" because it's easier and our fingers are tired from all the typing.

The Noise modifier generates a value using one of several gradient noise functions. This value can set a vertex's height, set a biome's strength, or serve as a mask input to another Noise modifier. The possibilities are endless.
Noise functions are a very complex topic, beyond the scope of this help text. The basics are below, but one of the best ways to learn is to experiment with the different noise types.
Most noise functions use five basic properties: Strength, Frequency, Octaves, Lacunarity, and Gain.
Strength Strength is the amplitude of the noise, probably the most intuitive setting. Increasing it makes the noise bolder (ie - it outputs larger values).
Frequency Frequency sets the number of cycles per unit length. In other words, small terrain details need a higher frequency and large details need a lower one.
Octaves Available for fractal noise, octaves define how many times the noise function runs. With each run, Strength is multiplied by Gain and Frequency by Lacunarity. A common setup is Gain at 0.5 and Lacunarity at 2, so each run halves the strength and doubles the frequency, adding more refined detail at less strength. Increasing octaves can make terrain look great, especially up close, but can also hurt performance, so use them with a hint of caution.
Gain As noted above, gain multiplies strength for each successive octave. Typically gain is less than one, since you want strength to drop per octave, but working with noise is an art form and sometimes you must break the rules to create truly unique terrain. Experiment and see what looks best!
Lacunarity Lack-You-Nare-Itty. At least that's how I say it. This multiplies frequency with each octave. Typically you want it above one, so frequency increases per octave and details become tinier and more refined.

Planet modifiers are grouped into passes. Each pass runs its planet modifiers one at a time before the next pass starts. Passes have different purposes and different input data available.
Biome Pass The first pass to run. It sets up the biome strength values, laying out where each biome sits on your planet. For example, an earth-like planet would give high biome strength to arctic biomes at the poles and higher strength to deserts and grasslands near the equator.
Height Pass Runs next, mainly responsible for setting the vertex's height value.
Height Biomes Pass Runs next for each biome identified in the Biome Pass. If multiple biomes have strength values, they're blended automatically based on their individual strengths. Being biome-specific, this pass is meant for biome-specific modifiers.
Height Final Pass Runs next, useful for common modifiers that must run after the biome-specific ones. A great place for the RadialFlatten modifier to smooth terrain for structures and launch locations. Not run for individual biomes.
Final Pass The last pass for the terrain, running after all other terrain passes. It sets any remaining unset vertex data, such as color. This is the only pass where the normal vector is available, and it should not modify the height.
Final Biomes Pass The Final Pass for biome-specific modifiers. Values are blended based on the strengths from the Biome Pass.
Water Pass Runs last. Sets water-related data such as color, wave intensity, etc.
Water Biomes Pass The Water Pass for biome-specific modifiers, with water properties blended based on the strengths from the Biome Pass. This is the last pass to run.

Here you can build a system using planets saved on your device. Select a planet to tweak its orbital parameters, adjusting the shape and size of its orbit. You can also add a child planet that orbits the selected one as a satellite.
The time panel in the top right corner lets you advance and reverse time to view how your planets move through their orbits.
The Locations flyout panel shows all locations on planets as they're added to the system. However, if you edit a planet's launch locations after adding it, they won't appear in the System's launch location list. Click the RESET button at the bottom of that panel to search all planets in the system and rebuild the list.

The Brush flyout lets you add custom maps to your planet. These maps can work alongside Noise modifiers or override the Noise output completely. For example, this is useful for painting continent locations by hand. Note that the planet must be configured to use a Planet Brush Map.

To make truly unique planets, you'll likely need the Terrain Generation flyout panel. It's the most complicated part of Planet Studio, but also the most powerful.
Terrain generation runs a list of planet modifiers for each terrain vertex. These modifiers calculate the vertex's height, color, texture data, etc.
Terrain Generation has two views: Basic and Advanced. Basic shows only a subset of modifiers, with a simplified inspector panel when selected. Advanced shows all modifiers and all their properties in the inspector. You can also view the Data Flow, which shows how data passes between modifiers; see the Data Flow section for details.
Basic is selected by default, but you can switch modes by tapping the button at the top left of the flyout panel.

trans-unit.source: Toggles a ring system on/off for the celestial body.
The inner radius of the planetary ring system, scaled by the planet radius. A value of 1 begins the rings at the surface of the celestial body.
The outer radius of the planetary ring system, scaled by the planet radius. A value of 2 ends the rings at a distance of one planet radius from the surface of the celestial body.

The texture for the rings. It should only need to be a single pixel tall (and any width you like). Textures taller than one pixel can be selected, but only a single row of pixels is actually used for the rings.
The euler angles defining the rotation of the rings relative to the celestial body.
Enter a file name to save the celestial body.
A celestial body already exists with that name. Do you wish to overwrite it?
Enter a file name to save the planetary system.
A planetary system already exists with that name. Do you wish to overwrite it?
A valid file name is required.
A planetary system must have at least one launch location.
This will restore launch locations from all celestial bodies in the planetary system.
Add a new terrain texture to this celestial body.

The constant value to add to or subtract from every pixel. Ideally, every texture should average 0.5 (from 0 to 1). A lower or higher average can greatly impact the average brightness of the terrain using that texture. This setting adjusts that average color if the source texture is too bright or dim.

Detail textures brighten or darken the terrain when above or below the 0.5 color value (range 0 to 1). This setting multiplies the difference between the pixel value and 0.5, effectively magnifying the texture's details.
Convert the texture to grayscale before sampling the red channel for the detail texture value used at runtime.
Planet has multiple splatmaps, which is not currently supported for editing.
Planet does not support terrain textures
Please confirm that you want to remove the last terrain texture from this celestial body.
Removes the last texture from this celestial body.

The base UV scale for the celestial body when the camera is near the surface. This shared setting affects both terrain and water. Texture mapping uses two UV sets: scaled UVs near the surface and non-scaled UVs farther away. The tiling level for non-scaled UVs is how many times the texture repeats over each of the planet's six faces. For scaled UVs, the tiling level is multiplied by this scaled UV size to get the repeat count. So if this is 256 and a scaled UV level's tiling is 2, the actual tiling for that level is 512.
The strength of the texture at this level (typically from 0 to 1).

One of the terrain textures used by the celestial body — up to 8 per body. Textures must be added here first, then selected on the Biomes flyout to choose where they're used on the surface. They act as detail textures, brightening and darkening the surface's base color. Only a single channel (red) is used: red values above 0.5 (on a 0 to 1 scale) brighten the terrain color, and values below darken it.

The distance adjustment value added to the distance that determines the tiling level. It is applied after the distance scalar.
Example: If the first tiling level lasts until about 100 meters and this adjustment is -500, the first tiling level will last until about 600 meters.
The distance scalar used to adjust the distance at which tiling levels begin. Doubling this value makes tiling levels begin twice as early as normal.
Regenerates the tiling numbers in the table below.
This will reset all tiling levels in the table below.

The tiling level at which textures switch from regular UVs to scaled UVs. Texture mapping uses two UV sets: scaled UVs closer to the surface and non-scaled UVs farther away. The non-scaled tiling level is how many times the texture repeats over each of the planet's six faces. The scaled tiling level is multiplied by the scaled UV size to give how many times the texture repeats.
The amount of tiling to apply to textures at this level. Lower levels are shown closer to the ground so more tiling is needed.

Toggles water on/off for the celestial body.
The sea level of the planet, relative to the planet radius.
The scalar applied to the specularity at this level.

The specularity scale of the water, typically between 0 and 1. It can change as the camera nears the surface. Each entry in this table, from bottom to top, represents the camera getting closer to the surface, with the top entry being the closest.
The strength of the texture at this level.

The strength of the water's normal map textures, typically 0 to 1. Strength can change as the camera nears the surface. Each entry in this table, from bottom to top, represents the camera getting closer, with the top being closest.

The texture tiling level for the water's normal map textures. Tiling changes as the camera nears the surface. Each entry in this table, from bottom to top, represents the camera getting closer, with the top being closest. Somewhere in the middle, based on the terrain splatmap's setting, the UV scale changes, so the tiling levels here must change too to compensate.
The movement speed of the texture at this level.

The speed of the water's normal map textures (not the actual waves). Speed can change as the camera nears the surface. Each entry in this table, from bottom to top, represents the camera getting closer to the surface, with the top entry being closest.
Sets the depth in meters at which the color gradient evaluates at its max value (on the right of the gradient).
The color gradient of the water. Water color is a gradient based on depth. The max depth for the gradient is configured with the setting below.
The intensity of the underwater color.
The underwater color used when the light is no longer visible.
Sets the density of the fluid in kg per m3.
The emissivity of the water. At 100% emissiveness, the water is unaffected by light.
The color of the water foam which is applied on top of reflection/refraction in very shallow water.
The maximum depth at which foam is applied.
The strength of the foam color.
The higher this value, the stronger the reflections will be at a given viewing angle.
The depth in meters at which the light from the sun can no longer pass.
The distance in meters from the camera at which underwater vision fades.
The metallicness of the water from a visual standpoint.
The higher the value, the more distortion in the water's reflections.
Controls the strength of the terrain and craft reflections on the water's surface.
The higher the value, the more distortion in transparent water due to refraction.

How strongly the planet's Resource Distribution modulates this sub-biome's resources. 0 gives uniform coverage across the biome (ice caps, salt flats); 1 gives full patchiness from the planet's distribution field. Ignored when the planet has no Resource Distribution modifier in its pipeline.
The sub-biome data used when the terrain is relatively flat (defined by the slope range setting).

trans-unit.note: Fits 338px at 16px. biome resource row label
Fits 338px at 16px. biome resource row label

trans-unit.source: The mineable resources present in this sub-biome. Each entry pairs a fuel id with a 0..1 concentration that the drill harvest rate is multiplied by. Multiple entries form a mixture — concentrations are independent multipliers, not a partition that must sum to 1.
The sub-biome data used when the terrain is relatively sloped (defined by the slope range setting).

The range over which terrain blends from the primary sub-biome data to the slope sub-biome data. The minimum value is where the slope data begins transitioning in and the primary data begins transitioning out. The maximum value is where the slope data reaches 100% strength and the primary data is no longer used. These values equal one minus the dot product of the normalized planet position (on a unit sphere) and the terrain's normal vector.

trans-unit.source: Congratulations on starting your own aerospace company! It's a tough business, but with my connections I can help you succeed. Please, allow me to introduce myself: I am Algernon Fizzlebottom.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial intro step 0 - welcome from Algernon Fizzlebottom

trans-unit.source: I recently inherited my grandfather's research company and own many technology patents. I don't have time to chase the stars myself, so I'm offering incentives to help new aerospace companies get started. Let's go to the Tech Tree and see what I can offer you.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial intro step 1 - directs user to the Tech Tree

trans-unit.source: Welcome to the Tech Tree. Click '{0}' to see what technologies it contains, then click Unlock. This one won't cost any Tech Points, so it's a great bargain.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial tech-tree first node prompt; {0} is the first node display name (e.g. Crew)

trans-unit.source: Fantastic! Now unlock '{0}'. It is also free.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial tech-tree second node prompt; {0} is the second node display name

trans-unit.source: Now it's up to you to choose your path. Start with '{0}' and build rockets, or start with '{1}' and build cars and planes? You only have enough Tech Points for one, so choose wisely!
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial tech-tree branching choice prompt; {0} is rockets node name, {1} is cars node name

trans-unit.source: You don't have access to any more technologies for now, so let me show you how to get more Tech Points. Click the back button at the top left to exit the Tech Tree.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial tech-tree exit prompt after all initial nodes are researched
MenuTutorial prompt directing the user to open the Career dialog from the main menu

trans-unit.source: Let's go back to Contracts and accept a contract. It's time to start your career!
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial prompt directing the user back to the Contracts tab

trans-unit.source: This is where you'll find contracts. Completing them earns the money you need to launch new crafts and unlock better launch locations. Your available funds show at the top of the screen.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial step 0 explanation shown when the Contracts tab is open
MenuTutorial prompt directing the user to click the Contracts tab

trans-unit.source: To use my patents, I need you to prove you deserve them. So I've set up these Milestones. Reaching them earns Tech Points, which you can spend to unlock new technology in the Tech Tree. Your Tech Point total is shown at the top of the screen.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial step 1 explanation shown when the Milestones tab is open
MenuTutorial prompt directing the user to click the Milestones tab

trans-unit.source: Here are the landmarks you can visit and additional milestones you can do in each Celestial Body. You can click them to see more details.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial step 2 explanation shown after the user selects Droo in Exploration

trans-unit.source: Here you can find the exploration related milestones. Click on Droo.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial prompt directing the user to click the Droo entry in Exploration
MenuTutorial prompt directing the user to click the Exploration tab

trans-unit.source: Select the {0} contract and then click Start Tutorial to accept this contract and begin a designer tutorial.
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial step 3 prompt asking user to select a specific contract; {0} is the contract name

trans-unit.source: Fantastic! I highly recommend doing the tutorial for this contract. Otherwise, click Build in the bottom left to enter the designer and start building your craft. Click Okay and get started! Good luck!
trans-unit.note: MenuTutorial final step 3 message shown after a contract is accepted

trans-unit.source: Would you like to back up your current craft before starting the tutorial?
trans-unit.note: DesignerTutorial intro confirmation prompt for backing up the user's craft

trans-unit.source: Welcome to the Designer! First, let me show you how to move the view around.
trans-unit.note: DesignerTutorial welcome message; reused for rotate/pan camera intro steps

trans-unit.source: This is the Command Pod and it's the brain of your rocket. Try to keep it safe. You can't control your rocket without it.
Before we add a part, let's turn on the Finger Tool. It makes placing parts with precision much easier. It can also help you clone parts, but we'll cover that later.
I've started with the car from The Jump tutorial but I've made some tweaks to make room for some wings.
First, we'll need to add the main wings that will provide the lift to get this beauty off the ground.
Now, add a control surface to this wing so the craft will be able to roll and turn while flying through the air.
trans-unit.note: FirstFlightTutorial step 3: add control surface to main wing

trans-unit.source: Use the Symmetry Tool and duplicate our work to the other side.
Now add the elevator, which will allow the craft to pitch upwards and downwards to change its altitude. It's quite important for airplanes.
The elevator's control surface should respond to Pitch input. Note to self: the wheels are also set to Pitch, so we'll change those later.
Use the Symmetry Tool and duplicate our work to the other side.
trans-unit.note: FirstFlightTutorial step 7: elevator symmetry (same English as Step4 but separate key for translator flexibility)

trans-unit.source: Now add the rudder, which provides stability on the yaw axis. It's a common misconception that the rudder is for turning — that's actually the job of the main wings rolling into the turn. The rudder is for minor corrections.
The rudder's control surface should respond to Yaw input.
Since the elevators use the Pitch input, we'll change the wheels' motor input to Throttle. Otherwise, pulling back on the stick to pitch up would also decrease the motor input.
trans-unit.note: FirstFlightTutorial step 10: configure motor input on wheels

trans-unit.source: When designing an airplane, the relationship between the Center of Mass (CoM) and the Center of Lift (CoL) is very important. We can visualize their positions using the View Panel.

As you can see, the red Center of Mass is slightly in front of the blue Center of Lift, so this craft should be aerodynamically stable. The further the CoM is in front of the CoL, the more stable it becomes, but it loses some maneuverability and pitch response.
The closer they are, the more aerobatic it becomes, but too close and it can turn unstable. CoM behind the CoL would be like trying to shoot an arrow backwards, feathers first.
To simplify: the red ball is in front of the blue ball, so this craft is good to go.
Great job! Even the Wright Brothers would be proud!
Now launch this magnificent creation from the Juno Village Runway. Let's see if this thing can fly!
We have a craft ready for you, but its engines need a few tweaks to improve performance so it can achieve orbit.

trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 2: open Design Info panel

trans-unit.source: This is the craft's total Delta V, meaning change in velocity. Theoretically, it's how fast the craft could go in a perfect environment with no gravity and no drag.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 2 DeltaV all-stages metric text

trans-unit.source: Realistically, we need at least 4,500m/s to reach low orbit around Droo. It looks like we have more than enough, but remember that engine performance is affected by atmospheric pressure, which changes with altitude.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 3: explanation about DeltaV requirement

trans-unit.source: We have some work to do. We'll look at each stage to see what we can do to improve performance. Don't worry, it's just rocket science.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 3 metric text after DeltaV at sea level

trans-unit.source: Let's look at the first stage, which consists of five solid rocket motors.
The Delta V looks okay for this stage. We just want it to gain some altitude before starting the more efficient engines, which need a thinner atmosphere to work.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 4 stage 1 DeltaV metric text

trans-unit.source: Another important metric is TWR, or Thrust to Weight Ratio. If it's less than 1, the craft can't overcome gravity during liftoff. This stage has plenty of TWR for launch.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 5 stage 1 Starting TWR metric text

trans-unit.source: Notice the Ending TWR is higher than the Starting TWR. That's because the engines burn fuel mass throughout the stage, so the craft loses mass. This means the rocket's acceleration actually increases throughout the stage.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 6 stage 1 Ending TWR metric text

trans-unit.source: One last thing: the Isp, or Specific Impulse. It's kinda like gas mileage for rocket engines, and higher is better. These solid rocket motors aren't very efficient, but they're cheap and get the job done.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 7 stage 1 Isp metric text

trans-unit.source: Let's look at the second stage. From our previous launches we have found that this stage will ignite around 8km altitude.

The Delta V and Starting TWR are terrible for this stage. That's because the Gnome Engine is optimized for a vacuum, but don't worry! We can do some rocket surgery here to improve its performance inside an atmosphere.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 8 stage 2 DeltaV metric text

trans-unit.source: This engine is suffering from severe over-expansion, which happens when the exhaust Exit Pressure is below Air Pressure. Over-expansion is what causes shock diamonds in the exhaust. The closer Exit Pressure is to Air Pressure, the more efficient the engine.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 9 stage 2 ExitPressure metric text

trans-unit.source: We can shorten the nozzle and crank up the power to raise this engine's Exit Pressure closer to the Air Pressure at this altitude.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 10: stage 2 configure rocket engine step

trans-unit.source: Let's take a look and see how things have changed.
That's a huge improvement in Delta V and TWR! Now let's take a look at the third stage.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 11 stage 2 review metric text

trans-unit.source: The third stage engine will mostly be working in the upper atmosphere and in space.
The Delta V is pretty good for this stage, but we can improve it by lengthening the nozzle.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 12 stage 3 DeltaV metric text

trans-unit.source: Ideally, Exit Pressure would be 0 for a rocket engine built to work in space, but that would need an infinitely large nozzle. We'll settle for something a little shorter than that.
trans-unit.note: FirstOrbitTutorial step 13: stage 3 configure rocket engine step

trans-unit.source: Great work! Now this rocket is ready for launch!
Click the launch button at the top right and launch from the Juno Village Pad.
Let's start with the same rocket we built for the Vertical Shot contract, minus the nose cone.
First, let's attach the payload. This is what the customer wants us to bring to space, so be careful with it and try not to damage it.
Now, let's add an 'Interstage'. It splits the rocket into multiple 'stages' but more on that later.
Now let's add another fuel tank below this, but we will make it a bit fatter so it can hold more fuel.
trans-unit.note: FirstPayloadTutorial step 4: add fatter fuel tank

trans-unit.source: Now let's connect an engine to this fuel tank.
Now let's duplicate this engine because we need more thrust.
trans-unit.note: FirstPayloadTutorial step 6: duplicate engine via symmetry

trans-unit.source: Now let's add some fins to the bottom stage for more stabilization. We can clone the fins from the upper stage to save us some work.
trans-unit.note: FirstPayloadTutorial step 7: add fins to bottom stage
FirstPayloadTutorial step 8: enable symmetry on fin

trans-unit.source:
Staging is normally calculated automatically, but it's a good idea to check it before launching.
The Second Stage Engine should actually be in Stage 2 so it can activate and do its thing before the payload is deployed.
trans-unit.note: FirstPayloadTutorial step 9 staging step main text

trans-unit.source: Excellent! You have built a multi-stage rocket!
Now click the Launch button and see how it flies.
Great news! We have an airplane for you, all ready to go!

These electric motors spin the propellers to generate thrust. They spin in opposite directions so the torque cancels out.

It's very efficient, but also a bit slow. Later, after you unlock jet engines, you'll be able to build much faster airplanes.
trans-unit.note: FirstRaceTutorial step 2: electric motor explanation; preserves literal <br><br> tags

trans-unit.source: Good luck on your first air race!
Launch from the Juno Village Runway.
Since we are building a craft that mostly moves horizontally, we'll need to change the Command Disc from Rocket to Plane configuration.
trans-unit.note: TheJumpTutorial step 1: command pod configuration step

trans-unit.source: Let's also increase the battery capacity, which will increase the driving range of this car.
Let's start building a car. First, add an empty fuel tank behind the Command Disc. This will serve as the body of the car.
trans-unit.note: TheJumpTutorial step 2: add fuel tank body

trans-unit.source: Now let's add a nose cone to help reduce drag and make it look cooler too.
Now let's add a front wheel.
Now let's add a rear wheel
trans-unit.note: TheJumpTutorial step 5: add rear wheel (intentionally no trailing period)

trans-unit.source: I think cars usually have wheels on both sides, so let's use the Symmetry Tool and duplicate our work to the other side.
Now do the same thing for the other wheel.

Make the front wheels turnable and reduce the engine torque to save money.
Since Symmetry Mode is enabled on this wheel, the other side automatically gets any changes we make.
trans-unit.note: TheJumpTutorial step 8: front wheel config; original had a paragraph break

trans-unit.source: Crank up the torque on those rear wheels and adjust their gear ratio. Lower gear ratios favor top speed; higher gear ratios favor acceleration.
trans-unit.note: TheJumpTutorial step 9: rear wheel torque/gear ratio config

trans-unit.source: Change the motor input to use Pitch instead of Throttle. This will allow you to go in reverse in case you get stuck.
Excellent! I've never seen a better car! I'm really proud of us!
Now click the launch button at the top right and launch this magnificent creation from the Juno Village Runway.
Let's build a rocket! The first step is to add a fuel tank below the Command Disc.
Now let's add a nose cone to help reduce drag.
Now connect an engine to this fuel tank. Engines draw fuel from the fuel tanks directly above them.
Now let's add some fins to help stabilize this beautiful creation.
Now we can enable Symmetry Mode on this fin so we can duplicate our work instead of having to add each fin individually.
trans-unit.note: VerticalShotTutorial step 5: enable symmetry on fin

trans-unit.source: Now let's enable the gyro on the Command Disc. The gyro can help to stabilize the rocket when it's in flight.
trans-unit.note: VerticalShotTutorial step 6: enable gyro on command disc

trans-unit.source: Excellent! You have built your first rocket!
Click the launch button at the top right and launch from the Juno Village Pad.
Let's start building. The first step is to add a fuel tank below the Command Pod.
Now let's connect a small engine to this fuel tank. Engines draw fuel from the fuel tanks directly above them.
Now let's connect an 'Interstage'. It splits the rocket into multiple 'stages' but more on that later.
Let's add another, larger fuel tank below the Interstage.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 4: add larger fuel tank

trans-unit.source: Connect a more powerful engine to this fuel tank.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 5: connect more powerful engine

trans-unit.source: We're going to add side boosters, but first we need to add a 'Side Interstage' that it can connect to.
Add another fuel tank here. If you have trouble connecting, try dragging your mouse directly on top of the Side Interstage part we just added.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 7: add side fuel tank

trans-unit.source: Add another engine under this side fuel tank.
Let's add a nose cone to help reduce drag.
Now we can enable Symmetry Mode on this part so we can duplicate our work over to the other side.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 10: enable symmetry on side interstage

trans-unit.source: Solar panels are fun, let's add some of those.
Let's enable Symmetry Mode on this Solar Panel Array to duplicate our work to the other side of the rocket.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 12: enable symmetry on solar panel

trans-unit.source: Like many other parts, the Solar Panel Array is highly customizable.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 13: solar panel array customization (original had trailing single newline)

trans-unit.source:
Staging is normally calculated automatically, but sometimes you need to re-arrange things. I purposely messed up the staging for this rocket, so we'll need to fix it.
The Pixie Engine shouldn't turn on until after the large boosters have jettisoned. To do that, we need to move it to the last stage.
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 14 staging step main text

trans-unit.source: Excellent! You have built a multi-stage rocket! You should check out the Flight Tutorial next to learn how to fly this masterpiece!
trans-unit.note: SandboxTutorial step 15: final info step (also reused for EndStep)

trans-unit.source: Let me show you how to get this craft into orbit. I may pause the game periodically so you'll have time to adjust the controls.
The Nav Sphere controls your craft's heading. With Heading Lock enabled, your craft always tries to point toward the blue triangle. The white cone is the direction your craft currently points.
%ActivateInstruction% to activate your first stage. This will activate your engines.
trans-unit.note: LevelFlightTutorial Step 0 EnsureStage - %ActivateInstruction% placeholder is replaced at runtime

trans-unit.source: Keep going until your altitude is about 1,000m.
Time to start a 'Gravity Turn' so we can start building up lateral speed while we climb.
Continue like this until your altitude is about 5,000m
Adjust your Gravity Turn to help increase our lateral speed.
Continue like this until your altitude is about 15,000m. We need a lot of lateral speed to get into orbit.
Adjust your Gravity Turn for even more lateral speed.
Continue like this until your active engines run out of fuel
Great! Now it's time to activate the next two stages, which will jettison those empty fuel tanks and then start your next engine.
%ActivateInstruction% to jettison your empty fuel tanks and engines.
trans-unit.note: LevelFlightTutorial Step 5 EnsureStage - %ActivateInstruction% placeholder replaced at runtime

trans-unit.source: %ActivateInstruction% again to start your next engine.
trans-unit.note: LevelFlightTutorial Step 5 EnsureStage - %ActivateInstruction% placeholder replaced at runtime

trans-unit.source: Now, let's take a look at Map View.
This is the Map View. First, let's zoom in on your craft.
The blue cone is your craft and the blue line is your predicted trajectory/orbit. The green arrow is your 'apoapsis,' the highest point along your orbit.
Awesome! Now we need to kill the engines and wait.
Wait until we are 30 seconds from the apoapsis to do our next burn
While we're waiting, I just wanted to say thanks for playing our game.
Now we need to Heading Lock our 'prograde.' Prograde just means the direction the craft is moving. This ensures we burn efficiently as we reach the peak of our orbit.
Continue like this until your engine runs out of fuel.
%ActivateInstruction% to jettison your empty fuel tank and engine.
trans-unit.note: LevelFlightTutorial Step 9 EnsureStage - %ActivateInstruction% placeholder replaced at runtime

trans-unit.source: %ActivateInstruction% again to start your last engine.
trans-unit.note: LevelFlightTutorial Step 9 EnsureStage - %ActivateInstruction% placeholder replaced at runtime

trans-unit.source: We're almost there. Now burn until the orange 'periapsis' arrow shows up. The periapsis is the lowest point in our orbit, and we want it well above the atmosphere.
Continue burning until the orange 'periapsis' arrow appears and is well above the atmosphere.
You did it! Now kill your engines.
Now let's activate those fancy solar panels

Add Parameter Parameters can be used to pass data into your custom expression/instruction when they are executed.
You must add some text before you can create a custom expression/instruction.
Custom expressions can combine expressions to return a value, but cannot execute instructions. They're similar to a function in functional programming.
Custom instructions define a sequence of instructions to run when called, but cannot return a value. They are similar to a procedure in imperative programming.

Once created, this definition block is placed in your program so you can define exactly what it returns. A new block is also added to the Custom Expressions panel on the left, which you can use to call/execute this expression in your program.

Once created, this definition block is placed in your program so you can define the exact instructions this custom instruction should execute. A new block also appears in the Custom Instructions panel on the left, which you can use to call this instruction in your program.
